name: micro-optimizations
intent: Find the small part of a program that actually costs the time - by measurement, never by intuition - change exactly one thing there, prove the change with a stable benchmark, and keep it behind a regression guard.
problem: Performance work is usually aimed at the wrong code. The loop that looks expensive is often 2% of the run, the real cost is a cache miss or an allocation in a helper called from everywhere, and nobody knows which because intuition has been the only guide. The result is a codebase full of contorted hot spots that bought nothing, code that is hard to read and hard to change, and a genuine bottleneck left untouched because nobody profiled. The discipline exists to convert an assumed cost into a measured one.
context: Applies after a system works and a measurement says it is too slow: a service with a p99 that misses its budget, a batch job that overruns its window, a game that drops frames, a mobile app that burns battery. It is the process that decides *which* of the catalog's technique records to apply - data-locality, small-object-optimization, prefetching, inline-functions, object-pool, shrink-to-fit - and it is the step that keeps them from being applied blind. It does not apply to designing for performance, to algorithmic complexity changes, or to guessing at speedups before anything has been measured.
benefits: It replaces intuition with measurement, which is the whole point: Knuth's own conclusion from seven years of measurement tools is that 'the universal experience of programmers who have been using measurement tools is that their intuitive guesses fail'.

Amdahl's law bounds every decision in advance, so effort can be spent only where the payoff is real: optimising the 80% of a program that is already 2% of the runtime cannot matter however clever it is.

It concentrates effort on the small part - Knuth's framing is that roughly 97% of the code should be left alone and the critical 3% deserves careful attention, which is a scope decision as much as a performance one.
One change at a time with a benchmark before and after makes each optimisation attributable and revertable, so a regression is caught at the change that caused it rather than three commits later.
A regression guard converts a one-off win into a permanent property: a benchmark in CI means the optimisation cannot silently rot as the surrounding code changes.

The cost model transfers between problems: once you know that a DRAM miss is ~80 ns and an L1 hit is ~1 ns, you can reason about where a win is available instead of measuring every candidate from scratch.
tradeoffs: Optimised code is by nature harder to change: a loop unrolled four times or a structure-of-arrays is faster and less obvious, and it is the code that will be broken by the next change to the logic.

Optimisation decisions are measured on one machine and one workload, so a win on the developer's laptop can be a loss on the production CPU, under a different input distribution, or with a different JIT version.
Benchmark infrastructure is a real cost: a harness that is stable, warmed up, statistically sound and run in CI is ongoing engineering, and a noisy harness produces confident nonsense.

The measurement can be actively misleading: a micro-benchmark that does not represent the production mix will confidently optimise the wrong thing, which is worse than not optimising because it is now hard to see.
Micro-optimisation is a local move in a system whose cost is often global: shaving 5% off a function that accounts for 1% of the runtime is 0.05%, and the review cost exceeds the benefit.
It invites over-fitting to a benchmark: once a benchmark is the target, the code can be made fast for the benchmark and slow everywhere else, and the benchmark stops representing the workload.

The honest ceiling is often disappointing: after the algorithmic and architectural work, the remaining wins are small, and a team can spend a quarter reaching a 15% improvement that users cannot perceive.

Knowledge of cost is unevenly distributed: the engineer who knows that a megamorphic call site or an unintentional allocation dominates has an advantage that is invisible in code review and hard to institutionalise.
quality_attributes_note: Observability is scored high because the pattern is measurement-first - a profiler and a benchmark are the mechanism, not an add-on. Extensibility and maintainability are the cost: optimised code resists change, which is precisely why the pattern insists on measurement and a regression guard rather than optimisation by default.

participants.responsibility: Produces the attribution that identifies the hotspot - where the time actually goes, at what granularity (function, line, allocation site).
participants.notes: The entry condition for the whole pattern: without it, every subsequent decision is a guess.

participants.responsibility: The measured small region that dominates the runtime - typically 3% of the code carrying most of the cost.
participants.notes: Identified by measurement, never by intuition; Knuth's data says intuition fails.

participants.responsibility: The prior knowledge that bounds the opportunity: an L1 hit is ~1 ns and a DRAM miss ~80 ns; the serial fraction caps the speedup.
participants.notes: This is what turns 'which optimisation is worth trying' into a decidable question.

participants.responsibility: One change at the hotspot - a layout change, an allocation removed, a branch removed, a call inlined, an algorithm swapped.
participants.notes: One at a time, so the before/after numbers are attributable.

participants.responsibility: A stable, warmed-up, statistically meaningful measurement of the before and the after, on representative input.
participants.notes: Its noise floor is the resolution of every decision the pattern makes.

participants.responsibility: The benchmark or performance test kept in CI so the win cannot silently rot as surrounding code changes.
participants.notes: This is what makes the optimisation permanent rather than a one-session change.

use_cases: A service whose p99 exceeds its budget: profile shows the tail is a specific call path, and the fix is a layout or allocation change at that path rather than a redesign.
A batch job overrunning its window: the profile attributes most of the runtime to one stage, and the optimisation targets that stage.
A game dropping frames: the frame profile names the hot function, and the fix is a data-layout change or an allocation removal there.
A mobile app's battery and frame budget: micro-optimisation of the per-frame allocations that the profiler attributes is the difference between smooth and janky.

Choosing between two equivalent constructs: knowing the relative cost of the alternatives makes the choice a free decision ('never give up your performance accidentally'), rather than an optimisation at all.
After a regression: a commit bisect plus a profile finds which change moved the hotspot, and the fix is reversed or amended rather than guessed at.
A library whose hot path is dominated by a cache miss: data-locality or prefetching applied at the measured hotspot rather than applied preemptively everywhere.
Establishing a performance budget in CI: the regression guard is itself the deliverable, so a future contributor cannot quietly undo the win.
avoid_when: Nothing has been measured yet - that is the definition of premature, and Knuth's whole argument is that the guesses fail.
The algorithmic complexity is wrong - an O(n^2) loop made constant-factor is still O(n^2); fix the algorithm first and the micro-optimisation may become unnecessary.
The cost is I/O or network - shaving instructions in the caller does nothing for a round trip; optimise the access pattern, the batching or the caching instead.
The profile says the code is not hot - by Amdahl's law the maximum possible win is bounded by its share of the runtime, so a clever change there is wasted effort.
The benchmark does not represent the production workload - a micro-benchmark optimised against becomes confidently wrong in production, which is worse than leaving it alone.
The change would obscure the logic beyond what a comment can repair, and the win is under a few percent - the readability cost exceeds the benefit.
A managed runtime's JIT already handles it: object allocation the escape analysis can remove, or devirtualisation the JIT performs, are not yours to micro-optimise by hand.
The team has no stable benchmark - without one, every 'optimisation' is a guess with extra steps, and the risk of a silent regression outweighs the chance of a win.
pitfalls: Optimising before profiling: the intuition-guided guess is wrong far more often than it is right, and the resulting code is harder to change for no gain.
Optimising cold code: a function on a rare path can be made twice as fast and the runtime will not move, because the arithmetic in Amdahl's law caps the win at its share.
Benchmark noise mistaken for a win: a one-shot timing with a cold cache, a cold JIT tier and a garbage-collection pause landing on one run will 'prove' a 20% improvement that is not there.
JIT warm-up ignored: measuring a managed-runtime function on its first call measures the interpreter or the unoptimised tier, not the code that will run in production.
Dead-code elimination measuring nothing: an optimised-away benchmark loop reports microseconds while the real code takes milliseconds, and the 'optimisation' is measured against fiction.
Several changes at once: with three edits and one benchmark, a regression is unattributable and the whole batch gets reverted - including the two edits that helped.
No regression guard: the win rots silently as the surrounding code changes, and without a benchmark in CI nobody finds out.
Optimising the abstraction away by hand: copying a body, special-casing one caller, or hand-unrolling a loop makes the next logic change harder, and the cost is paid by whoever comes next.
Chasing microseconds in a system whose latency is milliseconds of network: the whole effort is invisible to the user, and the real bottleneck is untouched.

related_patterns_notes.data-locality: The technique most often reached for after a profile, and the one that follows directly from the cost model: if the profile shows cache misses, arrange the data so the loop streams. This record owns the decision to apply it; data-locality owns the mechanism.
related_patterns_notes.small-object-optimization: A specific technique this record routes to: when the allocation profile shows per-object allocation dominating, storing the value inline is the fix. Applying it without a profile is the failure mode this record exists to prevent.
related_patterns_notes.inline-functions: Another routed technique, with its own trap (code size) that only a measurement can settle. This record decides whether the call overhead is worth attacking; inline-functions owns how.
related_patterns_notes.prefetching: The technique for latency-bound loops that data-locality cannot regularise. Reaching it requires a measurement showing the stall, because a prefetch in the wrong place actively costs performance.
related_patterns_notes.object-pool: The answer when the profile shows allocation dominating - and the answer when it shows allocation *not* dominating, in which case pooling is pure cost. The profile decides, which is why it belongs behind this decision.
related_patterns_notes.flyweight: Intrinsic-state sharing chosen by measurement: it trades a pointer chase for allocation, and which wins depends on the measured access pattern.
related_patterns_notes.copy-on-write: A structural alternative to micro-optimising a mutable update - publish a new immutable version with one pointer store, so the read path needs no optimisation at all. Often the better answer than hand-tuning a hot loop.
related_patterns_notes.double-buffer: The structural way to hide a latency by overlap rather than by shaving instructions, which is what a memory-bound profile should lead to.
related_patterns_notes.immutable-object: In managed runtimes, immutability is what lets the JIT remove allocations and share state, which is usually a larger win than any hand-optimisation - and it is a design choice made before measurement, not a tuning pass.

anti_patterns: Optimising before profiling: the guess-driven 'this loop looks slow' change, which Knuth's seven years of measurement data says is usually wrong.
Optimising the 97% instead of the 3%: careful work on code that carries 2% of the runtime, which Amdahl's law caps at a 2% win however clever it is.
Hand-unrolling and hand-inlining a hot loop 'because loops are slow', without a measurement and without an instruction-cache check - the classic premature micro-optimisation.
Declaring a win from a single timing run with a cold cache and no warm-up, producing a confident number that does not reproduce.
Making three changes and one benchmark, so a regression cannot be attributed and the whole batch is reverted.
Optimising an abstraction into special cases (one caller gets a hand-tuned copy) until the logic change becomes a cross-cutting edit.
Optimising around a symptom rather than the cause: shaving instructions in a caller whose cost is a network round trip.
Leaving no regression guard, so the win silently rots as the surrounding code changes and the next person redoes the work.
Applying a technique record (prefetching, inline-functions, object-pool) across the codebase 'to be safe', rather than at the one place the profile pointed to.
design_principles: Measure before changing: the attribution from a profiler is the entry condition, and intuition has been shown to fail.
One change, one measurement: a benchmark before and after a single edit is what makes the result attributable and revertable.
Let the cost model bound the effort: the memory-latency hierarchy and Amdahl's law say where a win can exist, so most candidates are excluded before any work.
Protect the win with a guard: an optimisation without a regression test is a temporary change that will be lost.
Keep the logic readable: an optimisation that cannot be understood by the next reader is a net loss even when it is faster.
best_practices: Profile before touching anything, and record the attribution (function, line, allocation site) alongside the change so the next person knows why this code is shaped that way.
Write the benchmark BEFORE the change, confirm it is stable across runs (the noise floor sets the smallest win you can honestly claim), then make exactly one change.
Warm up before measuring in a managed runtime: run the workload enough times for the JIT to reach steady state, or you are timing the interpreter.
Clean the cache state or measure it consistently between runs, and exclude GC pauses - an unrepresentative harness produces confident nonsense.
Check that the benchmark's output is not being optimised away; a black-hole benchmark reports microseconds and validates nothing.
Keep the regression guard: put the benchmark in CI with a threshold, so a future change cannot silently undo the win.
Sanity-check the opportunity with the cost model before starting: if the hotspot is 2% of the runtime, a perfect optimisation gains 2%, and that is not worth the readability cost.
Prefer the structural fix when one exists: immutability, copy-on-write or a double-buffer removes the cost entirely, where a tuned loop only reduces it.
Write the reason next to the code ('flat array: the profile showed pointer-chasing dominated') so the next change does not 'helpfully' reintroduce the pointer.

Between two equivalent constructs, take the cheaper one - that is a free decision informed by knowledge, not a premature optimisation, and it is what 'never give up your performance accidentally' means in practice.
sources: Donald E. Knuth, 'Structured Programming with go to Statements' (ACM Computing Surveys 6(4), 1974) - the primary source of 'we should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil', together with the two clauses that are usually dropped: 'yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%' and 'it is often a mistake to make a priori judgments about what parts of a program are really critical, since the universal experience of programmers who have been using measurement tools is that their intuitive guesses fail'. https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/356635.356640

Donald E. Knuth, 'An empirical study of FORTRAN programs' (Software: Practice and Experience, 1971) - the empirical origin of the profile as a table of statement frequency counts, and the conclusion that 'profile-keeping should become a standard practice in all computer systems', i.e. measurement as the basis of optimisation rather than intuition. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/spe.4380010203

Jeffery R. Ytterstrom, 'The Fallacy of Premature Optimization' (ACM Ubiquity) - the reading of Hoare and Knuth that preserves the 'about 97% of the time' clause, the distinction between premature optimisation and concern about performance, and Rico Mariani's 'never give up your performance accidentally' as the rule for choosing between equivalent constructs. https://ubiquity.acm.org/article.cfm?id=1513451

University of Alaska Fairbanks CS 641 lecture notes, 'Performance Modeling: Amdahl, AMAT, and Alpha-Beta' - the arithmetic that bounds any optimisation effort: Amdahl's law (on four cores, even 80% parallel code still spends half its time in the serial part) and Average Memory Access Time (AMAT = hit_rate x hit_time + miss_rate x miss_time), which is why a 5% miss rate against DRAM costs more than the arithmetic in the loop. https://www.cs.uaf.edu/2011/spring/cs641/lecture/04_05_modeling.html
